doc.title: Kidd Jordan interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 24, 2006

title: Skills for today's students; learning from mistakes in elementary band
summary: Students should write and score; Jordan lets children's scale mistakes lead to Lydian sounds.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Definitely. Does a student nowadays, an aspiring musician, need to have different skills than guys in the fifties or forties did?

Oh yeah, definitely. I think they need to know how to write, they need to know how to write scores, they need to get into all of it. And it’s easy enough ‘cause they got all the computers, like the computers have made a whole lot of people composers. I mean people can sit down and compose and listen at it and what have you. And you’ve got the notation they can do, I mean it’s easy enough. Although I’m not a computer person I’m still writing by hand and still doing all the other stuff, but I mean it made it much easier for them. So you know then they can aspire to write for films and all kinds of things. So I think the generation is going to be much better, but dealing with creative music I think they’ll always have that problem. Because the masters had it, they’re still having it, and I know in my lifetime and probably a hundred years after my life they’re going to be still having it. So it’s just a matter of taste I guess. There’s always going to be a few, pockets here, pockets there. And like I said some things isn’t for everybody. Some things are just for a chosen few. Because when Jesus had his disciples he picked twelve. I mean, it wasn’t for everybody, it was just for a chosen few. So some things are just for a chosen few. And when I go and play with the guys, wherever we play, the community, we got a good little community going. So you know I can go and play with them, ‘cause they know I’m going to play by ear anyway whatever they got. I can read it if they write it out, I can read it, but sometimes it makes my eyes too bad, I can’t do it, I just play. They say “oh man come on Kidd, read the book.” You know but it’s like I can hear something on it. And I like to do that with kids too because sometimes you write something and they start playing and they hear much better. Even if they’re making mistakes. And they don’t even hear where there’s mistakes and if they’re sounding good to me. I remember, I’ve got to tell you this. When I was teaching in the elementary school I was teaching them the scales. And some of them would play a C scale, then a C scale and a G scale. They would put the F sharp in the C scale. So man I’d be listening to it and it’d be wrong, I’d say wow, listen to this. And you know the story with the Lydian and all that, say yeah, they put the B flat in it and the F sharp and a B flat. I said I wouldn’t tell them the difference, I’d just be up there just letting them go. And I’d call and say, “now you’ve got to learn your scales” and when the band comes into and does that I wouldn’t even stop them. I’m

just sitting there listening saying “yeah, sounds good to me.” So you know out of mistakes. And some of them early kids who I taught that went on and they said, ‘yeah man, an F sharp and a D flat.” I said, “that’s right so now you hear it, you hear how it’s supposed to go.
They found a context for it.

They put the E natural in the B flat scale, yeah man, you got that flat five, raised fourth, and that sounded good. And it went on and it got to be a part of their language. So they’ll stumble into some things.
